title: Release job's QEMU/BuildKit images are pulled by mutable default tags and run privileged around the registry credentials
description: release.yml pins docker/setup-qemu-action (line 99) and docker/setup-buildx-action (line 102) by commit SHA but passes no 'image' input to setup-qemu and no driver/driver-opts to setup-buildx, so both fall back to whatever container images the actions default to at those SHAs. Upstream, these defaults have historically been docker.io/tonistiigi/binfmt:latest (run --privileged to register QEMU binfmt_misc handlers on the runner kernel) and a docker-container BuildKit builder from moby/buildkit:buildx-stable-1 (a privileged daemon that executes every RUN step of the multi-arch build, assembles and pushes the images, and obtains the Docker Hub/Harbor credentials stored by login-action through the buildx session when it pushes). If the defaults at the pinned SHAs are still tag references, whoever controls those Docker Hub tags (their third-party maintainers, or anyone who compromises those accounts) at release time can change the bytes of the published noixdev/pulsix-manager and pulsix-worker images on both registries, including the arm64 variants whose RUN steps (npm ci, go build of the manager and embedded agent binaries, pip/apt in the worker) execute under the registered QEMU interpreter, or capture the push credentials, with no change to this repository. Repository-side triggers and the guard job are sound (tag push is writer-only, ancestry and CI checks on github.sha, tag regex-validated via env); this is the one executable input of the privileged release build not covered by the SHA/digest pinning policy of backlog 1.32. The lower-trust actor is an upstream image publisher outside this repository's review, so impact is high but likelihood is low.
claimed_root_cause: The action SHA pins do not cover the container images those actions pull at runtime; release.yml sets no setup-qemu 'image' input and no setup-buildx driver-opts image, so binfmt and BuildKit are resolved from the actions' default (expected mutable tag) references instead of digests.

trace.description: A v* tag push (writer-only) starts guard and then the release job, which holds DOCKERHUB_TOKEN and HARBOR_PASSWORD.

Only 'platforms: arm64' is set; no 'image' input, so the action's default binfmt image (expected docker.io/tonistiigi/binfmt:latest) is pulled and run privileged to install QEMU handlers on the runner.
No inputs; the default docker-container driver starts a privileged BuildKit container from the action's default image (expected moby/buildkit:buildx-stable-1).

trace.scope: jobs.release.steps[Log in to Docker Hub] (and Harbor, line 115)
trace.description: Registry credentials are written to the runner's docker config; buildx serves them to the BuildKit daemon over the build session when it pushes.

trace.scope: jobs.release.steps[Build and push the manager image] (worker at line 133)
trace.description: The BuildKit builder builds linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 and pushes noixdev/pulsix-manager and pulsix-worker as :vX.Y.Z and :latest to Docker Hub and harbor.cloud.noidee.dev.

evidence.description: docker/setup-qemu-action@99012661954931238ded8c8b007157a8430204e1 # v4.4.0 with only 'platforms: arm64' (line 101); no image input.
docker/setup-buildx-action@f87e5991a6d7451dcb8d9637bfbc97413f497069 # v4.4.1 with no 'with:' block at all (no driver, driver-opts or version input).
platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64 for the manager (line 137 for the worker): arm64 stages execute under the QEMU handler registered by setup-qemu.

Build stage FROM golang:1.27.1-alpine@sha256:... without --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM, so for arm64 'go mod download', scripts/agent-binaries.sh and the manager go build (lines 53, 72, 79) run emulated; line 38 (node stage, npm ci/build) likewise.
Worker runtime stage FROM python:3.13-slim@sha256:... (and build stage at line 33) also without --platform, so arm64 RUN steps of the worker image run emulated.

Backlog 1.32 records SHA pinning of actions as the release-integrity policy; nothing in the repository pins the images these actions pull (grep for binfmt/buildkit/driver-opts/BUILDPLATFORM finds no other occurrence).

blockers: The default image references of docker/setup-qemu-action at 99012661954931238ded8c8b007157a8430204e1 and docker/setup-buildx-action at f87e5991a6d7451dcb8d9637bfbc97413f497069 (and any image caching behaviour such as setup-qemu's cache-image) are defined in those actions' sources, which are not in this repository and could not be fetched: the verifier's sandbox has no network access.

Hosted-runner behaviour is not observable locally: which image references (tag or digest) were actually pulled in past release runs, that the binfmt and BuildKit containers run privileged, and that the BuildKit daemon receives the registry credentials through the buildx session.

validation_plan.local: Read-only, no execution of target code: obtain the two action repositories at the pinned SHAs (owner side, since this needs network) and check `git show 99012661954931238ded8c8b007157a8430204e1:action.yml` for the default of the 'image' input (and 'cache-image') and `git show f87e5991a6d7451dcb8d9637bfbc97413f497069:action.yml` plus its src for the default driver and BuildKit image. The finding stands if either default is a tag without @sha256; it is refuted if both defaults are digest-pinned.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner check, non-destructive: in the logs of the most recent release run, expand the setup-qemu and setup-buildx steps and record the pulled image references and digests (e.g. 'docker.io/tonistiigi/binfmt:latest', 'moby/buildkit:buildx-stable-1') and whether the builder runs with --privileged. If they are tag references, pin them in release.yml: setup-qemu 'image: docker.io/tonistiigi/binfmt:<ver>@sha256:<digest>' (and cache-image: false if present), setup-buildx 'driver-opts: image=moby/buildkit:<ver>@sha256:<digest>' (or 'driver: docker' with the containerd image store), and consider FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM with GOOS/GOARCH cross-compilation in Dockerfile.manager's build stage so QEMU is out of the Go build path. Do not push a test tag to verify; review the workflow change instead.

title: Release tag workflow runs a cross-repo reusable workflow from a mutable @main with contents: write and all repository secrets
description: tag.yml grants GITHUB_TOKEN contents: write and calls NoiXdev/github-workflows/.github/workflows/create_go_changelog_version_release.yaml@main with secrets: inherit. It is the only workflow reference in .github/workflows that is not pinned to a full commit SHA. Both repositories are in the NoiXdev organization, so secrets: inherit applies. When a pulsix writer dispatches the workflow, whatever commit is on the shared repository's main at that moment runs with a contents: write token on pulsix and with every repository and organization secret pulsix can read. After the planned re-arm (backlog 1.38), the same happens automatically on every green ci run on main. Those secrets include DOCKERHUB_USERNAME/DOCKERHUB_TOKEN and HARBOR_USERNAME/HARBOR_PASSWORD. release.yml reads them in a job without an environment: key, so they are repository- or organization-level, not environment-scoped. Code holding those credentials can push noixdev/pulsix-manager and pulsix-worker images directly, including :latest, the compose default, and so bypass release.yml's main-ancestry and green-CI guard. Anyone who can change the shared repository's main is therefore a release authority for pulsix without any pulsix review. Today the called file is missing from that main, so a dispatch fails. Whoever first adds it there decides what runs. Creating a tag needs neither registry secret. Whether this crosses a trust boundary depends on whether the shared repository's main writers and protections are narrower than pulsix's release maintainers. That cannot be seen in source.
claimed_root_cause: tag.yml references the reusable workflow by a mutable branch ref (@main) instead of a reviewed commit SHA. That breaks the repository's own SHA-pinning policy (backlog 1.32), which every other uses: line in .github/workflows follows. The call also passes secrets: inherit instead of an explicit minimal secret list, inside a workflow whose top-level permissions are contents: write. Because the registry credentials are not scoped to a protected environment, the inherited set includes them.

trace.description: A pulsix writer can dispatch the workflow. The automatic workflow_run trigger on ci completing on main (lines 35-38) is commented out, and backlog 1.38 plans to re-arm it. The code that runs is chosen by the shared repository's main, not by pulsix.
Top-level permissions give the called workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN contents: write.
secrets: inherit passes every repository and organization secret available to pulsix, including the registry credentials release.yml uses, to a workflow in the same organization.
Runs NoiXdev/github-workflows' create_go_changelog_version_release.yaml at the mutable ref @main, the only unpinned workflow reference in the repository.

evidence.description: uses: NoiXdev/github-workflows/.github/workflows/create_go_changelog_version_release.yaml@main is a branch ref, not a commit SHA. A grep of every uses: line in .github/workflows finds no other reference without a 40-hex SHA.
secrets: inherit, with no explicit secret list.
DOCKERHUB_TOKEN is read in the release job, which declares no environment: key (lines 60-71). The secret is therefore repository- or organization-level, so secrets: inherit in tag.yml passes it on.
HARBOR_PASSWORD is read in the same environment-less job, so it is also passed on.
Backlog 1.32 records the SHA-pinning policy ('the SHA pinning was already in place and stays') in the same item that introduced tag.yml's @main call.
Backlog 1.38: the called file exists only on the shared repository's chore/pin-actions branch, with no pull request. The plan is to re-arm the automatic trigger once it reaches main.

blockers: Who can push, merge or force-push to NoiXdev/github-workflows' main is a hosted setting not visible in source: its collaborators and teams, branch protection and rulesets, required reviews, and bypass actors. The candidate is a real boundary crossing only if that set is broader or less protected than pulsix's own release maintainers.

Whether NoiXdev/github-workflows allows other organization repositories to call its workflows (Settings > Actions > Access) is a hosted setting. If access is not granted, the call fails closed and nothing runs.

validation_plan.local: Source-only, already settled. (1) grep -n 'uses:' .github/workflows/*.yml shows tag.yml:48 as the only reference not pinned to a 40-hex SHA. (2) release.yml's release job (lines 60-71) declares no environment:, so DOCKERHUB_* and HARBOR_* cannot be environment-scoped secrets. (3) tag.yml:43 and :49 grant contents: write and secrets: inherit. Nothing in the repository can show the shared repository's write access, so no local execution can decide the blocker. Do not dispatch the workflow or push a tag to test it, because that publishes.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner check, without dispatching anything. (1) In NoiXdev/github-workflows, list the users, teams and apps with write, maintain or admin access, and check main's branch protection and rulesets: required pull-request reviews, restricted pushers, force-push and deletion blocks, bypass list. Compare that set with the people allowed to release pulsix. (2) In NoiXdev/github-workflows, check Settings > Actions > General > Access to see whether pulsix may call its workflows. (3) In pulsix, and in the org's Settings > Secrets, confirm which secrets pulsix can read: DOCKERHUB_*, HARBOR_*, and any PAT used for tagging. The finding holds if the shared repository's main can be changed by anyone outside pulsix's release maintainers, or without a required review. Fix: pin the call to a full commit SHA of a reviewed shared-workflow revision, with a version comment. Replace secrets: inherit with an explicit list of only what tagging needs, which excludes the registry credentials. Move DOCKERHUB_* and HARBOR_* into a protected 'release' environment that only release.yml's release job uses.

title: Agent certificate renewal racing an admin revocation re-creates the agent registration with a fresh unrevoked certificate
description: Renew (internal/agentapi/service.go:237) trusts the interceptor's earlier serial lookup (internal/grpcsrv/auth.go:225-235) and then, after signing the CSR, calls agents.Register unconditionally. SQLStore.Register upserts host_agents, revokes the host's serials that are still unrevoked, and inserts the new serial with revoked_at NULL. If POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/agents/{host_id}/revoke (agents.Service.Revoke -> SQLStore.Revoke: revoke all certificates, delete host_agents) commits after the interceptor's lookup and before Register's upsert, Register inserts a new host_agents row for the new serial. LookupAgentSerial then resolves that serial as live. Revoke's CloseHost cuts the old streams, but the agent reconnects with the new certificate and keeps authenticating, streaming facts and check results, and renewing. The handler also set the host's monitored flag to false, so the UI shows the agent as revoked while it is still connected. Only the timing is uncertain. If Register commits first, Revoke revokes the new serial too and the outcome is safe. AgentStream closes the same window with a post-track GetBySerial re-check (stream.go:56-65). Renew has no such check, and grpcsrv has no renewal rate limit, so a holder of the agent key can call Renew repeatedly to widen its chance of hitting the window.
claimed_root_cause: agentapi.Service.Renew (service.go lines 237-260) never re-checks, after signing, that the presenting serial is still the host's active, unrevoked certificate before calling Register. SQLStore.Register (store_sql.go lines 151-174) and UpsertHostAgent (agents.sql lines 61-70, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (host_id) DO UPDATE) have no guard such as 'existing row present AND cert_serial = presented serial AND that certificate revoked_at IS NULL'. Register therefore re-creates a row that a concurrent Revoke deleted. The transaction uses the default READ COMMITTED isolation (pool.Begin in internal/db/scope.go), which does not serialize the two transactions.

trace.description: The mTLS interceptor resolves the agent's presented serial and refuses unknown or revoked serials (line 233). This is the only liveness check before the Renew handler runs.
A concurrent admin revocation calls agents.Service.Revoke. SQLStore.Revoke (store_sql.go line 239) marks every certificate of the host revoked and deletes the host_agents row in one transaction.
The new certificate is signed for the identity resolved earlier by the interceptor. Liveness is not re-checked before Register (line 250).

UpsertHostAgent re-inserts the host_agents row that Revoke deleted. InsertAgentCertificate (line 165) adds a new serial with revoked_at NULL, which LookupAgentSerial (agents.sql line 97 join) resolves as live.

evidence.description: Register is called without re-checking that agent.Serial is still live and still the host's active serial.
The sibling AgentStream re-reads the serial after tracking specifically to close the revocation race. Renew has no equivalent.
ON CONFLICT (host_id) DO UPDATE re-creates, without any precondition, a host_agents row that Revoke deleted.
The new serial is inserted with revoked_at NULL regardless of the presenting serial's state.
Revoke deletes host_agents and revokes certificates, but nothing stops a Register that runs afterwards from undoing the deletion.
WithWriteTx begins with pool.Begin (default READ COMMITTED), so the Revoke and Register transactions are not serialized against each other.

blockers: The decisive Postgres interleaving (SQLStore.Revoke commits between the interceptor's GetBySerial and SQLStore.Register's UpsertHostAgent) needs internal/db/testdb (testcontainers plus the host Docker socket), which the approved sandbox forbids. Only the in-repo fake store was exercised. Hunter artifact agents/h01-agent-facts/artifacts/evidence.txt shows Renew succeeding after Revoke, a live new serial, a restored registry row, and a second Renew accepting the post-revoke certificate. The SQL shape is the same in source.

The real width of the window (interceptor lookup, then CSR signing, then the Register upsert, against the revoke commit) under a real deployment was not measured. Exploitation also requires the attacker to hold the agent's private key (a compromised or malicious host agent).

validation_plan.local: Add an integration test (internal/agentapi or internal/agents) against internal/db/testdb with the real agents.SQLStore and agents.Service. Enroll an agent. Wrap the AgentSigner so that SignAgentCSR first runs agents.Service.Revoke(org, host) on the real store before returning, then call Renew with the enrolled certificate's identity in context (or over bufconn through the real interceptor). Confirmed if all of the following hold: Revoke returns nil; Renew returns OK; GetBySerial(newSerial) returns Revoked=false; GetByHost finds the host again with cert_serial = newSerial; a second Renew authenticated with the new certificate succeeds. Refuted if Renew fails or the new serial resolves as revoked or not found. Then verify the fix the same way. Either re-check GetBySerial(agent.Serial) inside Register's transaction and refuse with Unauthenticated when it is revoked or not found, or make UpsertHostAgent an UPDATE ... WHERE host_id = $1 AND cert_serial = <presented serial> that requires one affected row with that certificate's revoked_at IS NULL, so a deleted row is never re-inserted.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed and non-destructive, on a staging manager with a dummy host. Enroll a test agent. Have it call Renew in a loop while an admin calls POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/agents/{host_id}/revoke. Then query agent_certificates for that host (SELECT serial, revoked_at FROM agent_certificates WHERE host_id = <dummy>) and host_agents. Any unrevoked serial, or a host_agents row present after the revoke returned 200, confirms the race.

title: Auth rate limit checks before the handler and charges after it, so concurrent TOTP guesses from one address get past the failed-attempt budget
description: authRateLimitMiddleware first asks the limiter whether the address has already used up its budget. It then runs the handler and charges a failure only after the handler returns. Nothing reserves a slot before the handler runs. So every request that arrives before enough failures have been charged gets past the gate. A caller who has the victim's password, and so a pending session, can send large concurrent bursts of POST /api/v1/auth/totp/verify in each one-minute window. The configured limit is 20 failed guesses per minute (PULSIX_AUTH_RATE_LIMIT default), but a burst is limited only by how many requests the server accepts at once. The source has no per-account TOTP failure counter or lockout, so this per-address budget is the only limit on guessing the 6-digit second factor. Each guess matches one of 3 accepted time steps (skew 1). The same middleware also guards login, passkey login finish and invite accept.
root_cause: internal/api/auth_rate_limit.go:75-82 calls lim.Refused(ip) before next(ctx) and lim.Charge(ip) after it. Refused only reads the count (internal/clientip/limiter.go:77). Charge (internal/clientip/limiter.go:94) runs in a separate locked section. The budget is therefore never reserved for attempts that are still in flight. /auth/totp/verify (internal/api/mfa_handlers.go:148-160) has no other per-account attempt limit.
intended_behavior: At most PULSIX_AUTH_RATE_LIMIT failed attempts per address per minute should reach the TOTP verify, login, passkey-login and invite-accept handlers, however many requests are in flight at once. That is the limit documented at internal/config/config.go:68-77 and in the middleware's doc comment (internal/api/auth_rate_limit.go:46-62).

trace.description: A pending session (password already proven) submits a TOTP or recovery code. The route is registered with withAuthRateLimit(deps) at line 160.
lim.Refused(ip) only reads the counter. It refuses only when the charged count is already at the limit.
Checks the count under the mutex and changes nothing, so no slot is reserved for this attempt.
The handler (verifyFactorCode, then TOTP.Verify) runs for every request that passed the check.
A failure is charged only after the handler returns. By then every concurrent attempt has already been checked against the secret.

evidence.description: next(ctx) sits between the Refused check (line 75) and the Charge (line 82).
Charge caps the count at the limit and runs in its own locked section, separate from Refused.
verifyAndConsume compares the code against 3 steps (skew 1). A miss returns false at lines 289-291 and consumes nothing. No per-account failure counter exists in internal/auth or internal/api.
DefaultAuthRateLimit = 20 failed attempts per minute per address, per endpoint, is the only bound the code intends.

conditions.description: The attacker has the victim's password, or some other pending session that has not completed MFA, which is needed to reach /auth/totp/verify. Login brute force is also affected, but each attempt there costs an argon2id hash.
PULSIX_AUTH_RATE_LIMIT > 0 (default 20). The limiter is in-process, one per manager.

The requests must be in flight at the same time, before enough failures have been charged. Burst size depends only on the attacker's connections and on how many requests the server accepts and queues at once.

execution.attacker_perspective: A client with a pending session for an account protected by TOTP sends a burst of concurrent wrong-code verify requests from one address.
payloads: internal/api/v04_ratelimit_test.go (scratch copy only): a huma POST /verify route on chi/humachi behind the production withAuthRateLimit(Deps{AuthRateLimit: 20, ClientIP: clientip.New(nil)}). The handler sleeps 5 ms and returns 401, standing in for a wrong TOTP code. The route is served over loopback with httptest.NewServer. The test sends 50 sequential requests to one server, then 200 concurrent requests (released together, no barrier in the handler) to a fresh server, then one follow-up request.
instructions: Copy the repository into scratch and delete internal/api/*_test.go in the copy, because those tests import the database harness. Add the harness test there.

Run go test -count=1 -v -run TestV04AuthRateLimitConcurrent ./internal/api/ in the approved Docker sandbox: golang:1.27.1-alpine, --network none, read-only source and module cache, env -i allowlist, cap-drop ALL, uid 65532, 300 s timeout. Write stdout to evidence.txt.
execution.observed_result: Sequential: limit=20, 50 attempts, 20 reached the handler (20x 401, 30x 429). Concurrent: limit=20, 200 attempts from one address, 198 reached the handler (198x 401, 2x 429). After the burst the next request got 429. Source: agents/v04-session-auth/artifacts/evidence.txt. This independently reproduces the hunter's result (40 of 40 against a limit of 3, with a barrier), here with the default limit, real HTTP and no barrier.

remediation.strategy: Reserve the attempt atomically before the handler runs: claim the slot under the limiter mutex and refund it on 2xx, 5xx or 429. Also add a per-account counter or lockout for failed second-factor attempts on /auth/totp/verify that does not depend on the client address.

likelihood.reason: The attacker first needs the victim's password, then must keep sending large concurrent bursts. Each guess succeeds with probability of about 3e-6, so a meaningful chance of takeover takes hundreds of thousands of guesses, spread over many one-minute windows.

impact.reason: It defeats the second factor on an account whose password is compromised. The result is an MFA-complete session with that user's org roles, and instance-admin rights if the user has them.

confidence.reason: The production middleware and limiter ran unchanged in a sandboxed harness. With the default limit of 20, 198 of 200 concurrent failed attempts reached the handler, while sequential attempts were held to exactly 20. A source review found no per-account TOTP attempt limit that would add a second brake.

title: Session id is not rotated on MFA completion, so a planted pending session is upgraded by the victim's own second factor
description: Password login creates a session that is not MFA-complete. POST /api/v1/auth/totp/verify upgrades that same session row in place (mfa_complete=true, mfa_at=now()) and sends no new cookie. TOTP enrolment confirmation and passkey-registration completion do the same through completeEnrolment. Sessions are not bound to client IP or user agent, and the cookie name has no __Host- prefix. Suppose an attacker who knows a victim's password creates a pending session for the victim's account and can also place that cookie in the victim's browser for the Pulsix host, for example with a Domain-scoped, Path=/api cookie set from a sibling subdomain, or over plain HTTP when the deployment has no HTTPS or HSTS. The SPA's /auth/me call then sees the pending session and sends the victim to /login?step=totp. The victim's valid code makes the attacker's copy of the session MFA-complete, and it also counts as a fresh factor for step-up. The in-place upgrade is clear from source. Whether the attack works depends on whether the deployment gives an attacker a way to inject the cookie.
claimed_root_cause: Sessions.MarkMFAComplete (internal/auth/session.go:115, query MarkSessionMFAComplete at internal/db/queries/auth.sql:28) raises assurance on the existing session id. It does not revoke the session and issue a new id and secret. The verify handler returns okOutput with no Set-Cookie. The cookie is named pulsix_session with no __Host- prefix (internal/auth/middleware.go:13, internal/api/auth_handlers.go:160), and the application sends no HSTS header. Nothing stops a cookie of the same name planted from a sibling host or over plain HTTP from being chosen by r.Cookie, which takes the first match.

trace.description: The victim's browser submits its TOTP code together with whichever pulsix_session cookie it sends first. This route accepts pending sessions through requireSession.
r.Cookie(CookieName) takes the first pulsix_session cookie. A planted cookie with a longer path (Path=/api) is sent ahead of the victim's host-only Path=/ cookie.
The code is checked against p.UserID, the owner of the planted session, which is the victim's account. The victim's genuine code therefore passes.
The same session id is marked mfa_complete and mfa_at is set to now. No new credential is issued, so the attacker's copy of the cookie is now fully authenticated and fresh for step-up.

evidence.description: UPDATE sessions SET mfa_complete = true, mfa_at = now() WHERE id = $1 upgrades the row in place without changing id or secret_hash.
The verify handler returns &okOutput{} without setting a cookie, so the session credential is the same before and after the assurance change.
sessionCookie sets Name pulsix_session, Path=/, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, and Secure only when PublicURL is https. There is no __Host- prefix.
completeEnrolment also upgrades the existing session id in place after a passkey registration finishes.
ConfirmTOTP upgrades the existing session id in place inside the enrolment transaction.
The sessions table has only id, user_id, secret_hash, mfa_complete and timestamps. No client binding such as IP or user agent limits where a copied cookie can be used.
When a pending session already has a factor, the SPA routes it to /login?step=totp, which prompts the victim to enter the code.

blockers: The attack requires an attacker who can set a pulsix_session cookie in the victim's browser for the Pulsix host. That needs a same-site sibling subdomain the attacker controls, plain-HTTP access without HSTS (the application sends no HSTS itself), or another injection position. These are facts about the deployment and DNS, not about the repository.

The attacker must already know the victim's password to create the pending session for the victim's account. The cookie ordering (longer path sent first) and the SPA prompt flow are browser behaviour that cannot be observed in the approved sandbox. The DB-backed apitest harness cannot run there either, so even the server-side lack of rotation is established from source only.

validation_plan.local: In an environment that can run the apitest harness against a real Postgres: create user A with a confirmed TOTP factor. Log in with the password and record the pending cookie C. Call POST /api/v1/auth/totp/verify with cookie C and a valid code, and assert that the response has no Set-Cookie. Then call GET /api/v1/auth/me with the original C and assert mfa_complete=true. A fix should make C return 401 after verify, and the verify response should set a new session cookie.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner checks whether any less-trusted host shares the Pulsix registrable domain and could set Domain cookies, and whether the reverse proxy enforces HTTPS and HSTS with includeSubDomains. If injection is possible, the owner can test in their own test browser with dummy accounts: set a Domain-scoped pulsix_session cookie with Path=/api holding a pending session for a test account, confirm the SPA shows the TOTP prompt, enter the test account's code, and check that the planted cookie now reports mfa_complete=true on /api/v1/auth/me.

title: One tenant's duplicate playbook path blocks creation of a shared job template for every organization
description: InsertProjectedTemplates (internal/db/queries/shared.sql:316-321) writes one projected job_templates row per organization by LEFT JOINing that organization's playbooks rows at the definition's playbook_path, and assumes there is at most one per (org_id, repo_id, path). Nothing enforces that. The playbooks table (00018_jobs.sql:32-40) declares only PRIMARY KEY(id) and UNIQUE(org_id, id), and no later migration adds a constraint or index on playbooks. POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/playbooks (operator, PermPlaybooksWrite) calls playbooks.Service.CreateRepo. CreateRepo only checks the path's shape and that the repository exists in the org (repos.Get also returns the org's projection of a shared repository). It then inserts a new row unconditionally, so calling it twice with the same repo_id and path stores two rows. When the instance admin later creates a shared template that names this shared repository and path, the LEFT JOIN yields two rows for that organization that carry the same generated id i.id and the same name. The INSERT fails with a unique violation (job_templates PRIMARY KEY id / UNIQUE(org_id, name), 00018_jobs.sql:43,48). CreateTemplateWithProjections (store_sql.go:461-467) passes the error to collisionFromTemplateRace. Because Service.CreateTemplate's pre-flight check has already ruled out a real name collision, that function falls through to a bare ErrNameTaken (store_sql.go:497), and the shared handler maps it to HTTP 409 'name already in use' (shared_handlers.go:609-610). withTx rolls back the definition and every organization's projection. Result: an operator in one tenant, on purpose (by pre-registering likely paths such as site.yml, since the file need not exist) or by accident, stops the instance admin from distributing that shared template to every other tenant. The error names neither the organization nor the cause. The single-organization InsertProjectedTemplate (shared.sql:327-335) and UpdateProjectedTemplate (shared.sql:383) use a scalar subquery with LIMIT 1 and are not affected, so the problem is limited to the initial create. Impact is limited to availability of one instance-admin operation. It does not disclose or change data across tenants.
claimed_root_cause: The bulk projection query relies on a uniqueness assumption (one playbook per org/repo/path). Neither the schema (playbooks lacks UNIQUE(org_id, repo_id, path)) nor playbooks.Service.CreateRepo enforces it. Unlike the single-org InsertProjectedTemplate and UpdateProjectedTemplate, which use a scalar subquery with LIMIT 1, the bulk LEFT JOIN in InsertProjectedTemplates has no LIMIT, DISTINCT ON or per-organization aggregation. Duplicate rows a tenant controls therefore fan out the per-organization insert into a PK/unique violation that rolls back the installation-wide create.

trace.description: Gated by requireOrg(PermPlaybooksWrite), so operator or above. The caller sends the repo_id of the org's projection of a shared repository and a path. Calling it twice with the same values calls deps.Playbooks.CreateRepo each time.
Checks only the path pattern and that the repository exists in the org (repos.Get, which includes shared projections). It does not check for an existing playbook at the same repo and path.
Inserts a new playbooks row with a fresh UUIDv7 on every call (CreatePlaybook is a plain INSERT with no ON CONFLICT).
Only PRIMARY KEY(id) and UNIQUE(org_id, id). There is no uniqueness on (org_id, repo_id, path), so both duplicate rows are accepted. No later migration adds an index or constraint on playbooks.

The instance admin creates a shared template that names that shared repo and path. One InsertProjectedTemplates statement runs for every organization inside the same transaction as CreateSharedTemplate.

LEFT JOIN playbooks pb ON pb.org_id = o.org_id AND pb.repo_id = g.id AND pb.path = @playbook_path AND pb.source = 'repo' matches both duplicate rows. That emits two job_templates rows for the same org with the same i.id and name, which violates job_templates PRIMARY KEY(id) and UNIQUE(org_id, name).

The unique violation goes to collisionFromTemplateRace. No organization holds the name, so it returns bare ErrNameTaken (HTTP 409 'name already in use'), and withTx rolls back the definition and every organization's projection.

evidence.description: Bulk INSERT ... SELECT over unnest(ids) and unnest(org_ids) zipped by ordinality, with LEFT JOIN git_repos and LEFT JOIN playbooks. It has no LIMIT, DISTINCT ON or GROUP BY per organization, so every matching playbooks row repeats i.id.

The single-organization sibling InsertProjectedTemplate resolves the same playbook with a scalar subquery and LIMIT 1, so it tolerates duplicates. UpdateProjectedTemplate (line 383) does the same. Only the bulk create path fans out.
playbooks declares only UNIQUE (org_id, id). grep over internal/db/migrations finds no later unique index or ALTER that constrains (org_id, repo_id, path).
CreatePlaybook is a plain INSERT INTO playbooks with no ON CONFLICT clause.
CreateRepo calls s.store.Create unconditionally after the repository lookup and never refuses a duplicate path.
job_templates.id is PRIMARY KEY and line 48 adds UNIQUE (org_id, name). Two rows in one INSERT with the same id and name must raise SQLSTATE 23505.
collisionFromTemplateRace falls through to bare ErrNameTaken when no organization holds the name, which hides the real cause and the organization responsible.
shared.ErrNameTaken is mapped to huma.Error409Conflict('name already in use').

blockers: The decisive observation (the duplicate-row fan-out raising 23505 inside InsertProjectedTemplates, and the transaction rolling back for every organization) needs a running Postgres. The only local harness is internal/db/testdb, which starts Postgres through testcontainers over the host Docker socket. The approved offline sandbox forbids that, and no DB-backed package (internal/shared, internal/playbooks, internal/api) may run under it. The claim therefore rests on source and standard Postgres INSERT ... SELECT semantics, not on an observed run.

validation_plan.local: In a DB-enabled test environment (internal/db/testdb), add an internal/shared store integration test. 1) Create two dummy organizations A and B. 2) Create a shared repo definition through SQLStore so that both orgs get a git_repos projection. 3) In org A, call playbooks.SQLStore.Create twice with source='repo', the org-A projection's repo_id and path 'site.yml' (or call playbooks.Service.CreateRepo twice). 4) Call shared.Service.CreateTemplate with SharedRepoID set to that definition and PlaybookPath 'site.yml'. Expect today: errors.Is(err, shared.ErrNameTaken) is true and not a *NameCollisionError, zero rows in shared_job_templates, and zero job_templates rows with shared_template_id set for either org. Regression after the fix (DISTINCT ON (o.org_id) or a LATERAL ... LIMIT 1 in InsertProjectedTemplates, plus an additive UNIQUE(org_id, repo_id, path) WHERE source='repo' with a duplicate refusal in CreateRepo): the create succeeds and each org gets exactly one projection. No destructive steps; dummy data only.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed on a staging instance only. As an operator of a test org, register the same playbook path twice via POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/playbooks against that org's projection of a shared repository. Then, as instance admin, create a shared job template on that shared repository and path. Confirm the 409 'name already in use' and that a second test org received no projection. Afterwards, delete the duplicate test playbook rows.

title: Agent-reported host facts are rendered as trusted Ansible hostvars, so a monitored host can run commands on the org's worker controller
description: A host agent's Facts push stores arbitrary strings (up to 512 bytes, up to 64 keys) in hosts.facts. Every job's inventory snapshot then renders them verbatim as _meta.hostvars.<host>.pulsix_facts with no unsafe marking. The worker writes that document unchanged and passes an executable exec-cat wrapper as --inventory, so ansible-core 2.21.4 (the worker image pin) loads it through the script inventory plugin, which treats hostvars strings as trusted templates. When a play evaluates pulsix_facts (the documented purpose of the variable), a Jinja expression or lookup planted in a fact is evaluated in the Ansible controller process on the zone worker. Whoever controls one monitored host's agent identity (root on that host, or its agent certificate and key) can therefore execute commands as the run's play identity on the worker, with access to the material that run is given for every host in its scope. The webhook extra-vars path already neutralises exactly this with ansiblevars.Inert; the agent-facts path does not.
root_cause: renderer.hostVars assigns h.Facts unchanged to vars["pulsix_facts"] (internal/inventory/render/render.go line 390). agents.Service.RecordFacts validates only key count, empty keys and value length, and neither the manager nor the worker's mergeInventory wraps agent-originated strings as {"__ansible_unsafe": ...}, so ansible-core's script inventory treats them as templates.
intended_behavior: Data reported by a host agent is lower-trust than the controller and must reach Ansible as inert data: every string under pulsix_facts should be wrapped as {"__ansible_unsafe": ...} (ansiblevars.Inert), as webhook variables already are, so it renders literally and is never evaluated.

trace.description: The mTLS-authenticated agent's Facts message values are forwarded to the FactsSink, bound to the agent's own org and host from the interceptor-resolved identity.
After checking only key count, non-empty keys and value byte length (line 75), values containing Jinja delimiters are passed to the store.
Values are JSON-encoded (line 261) and merged verbatim into hosts.facts via UpsertHostFacts (jsonb ||, internal/db/queries/agents.sql line 111).
The stored host facts are passed into render.Host.Facts for the job's inventory snapshot.
Facts are emitted as _meta.hostvars.<host>.pulsix_facts with no __ansible_unsafe wrapping.

mergeInventory only adds connection variables; the document is written unchanged as the inventory document, and the exec-cat wrapper (layout.go line 136) is passed as --inventory (runner.go line 193).

The pinned ansible-core treats script-inventory hostvars strings as trusted templates; evaluating pulsix_facts renders the planted expression, including lookup('pipe', ...), in the controller process.

evidence.description: vars["pulsix_facts"] = h.Facts with no ansiblevars.Inert wrapping.
The only value check is a byte-length bound; content is unrestricted.
The inventory reaches Ansible through an exec-cat script, i.e. the script inventory plugin.
Inert exists and is applied to webhook extra vars (internal/jobs/run_overrides.go line 75), but not to facts.

The worker pins ansible-core 2.21.4; in that image a full ansible-playbook run against the rendered document evaluated the fact's Jinja and pipe lookup, while the __ansible_unsafe-wrapped control stayed literal.

conditions.description: The attacker holds a valid agent identity for one monitored host: root on that host, or its agent certificate and key.
The host is managed (rendered into job inventories) and a play run against it evaluates pulsix_facts, directly or through hostvars.
An operator, schedule or trigger runs such a play after the malicious facts push.

execution.attacker_perspective: Root on one host monitored by the Pulsix agent, sending a Facts message over that agent's own mTLS stream.
payloads: Facts{values: {"os": "debian-{{ 6 * 7 }}-uid{{ lookup('pipe', 'id -u') }}"}}

Rendered inventory: {"_meta":{"hostvars":{"web-1":{"ansible_host":"127.0.0.1","pulsix_facts":{"os":"debian-{{ 6 * 7 }}-uid{{ lookup('pipe', 'id -u') }}"}}}},"all":{"children":["ungrouped"]},"ungrouped":{"hosts":["web-1"]}}
Playbook task: ansible.builtin.debug: msg="host os is {{ pulsix_facts.os }}" (hosts: web-1, gather_facts: false)
instructions: In a scratch copy of the repo, a test in internal/inventory/render calls the real agents.Service.RecordFacts (fake store) with the payload fact, then render.Render for a managed host carrying the stored fact, and prints the document (golang:1.27.1-alpine, --network none, read-only, cap-drop ALL, user 65532, prescribed limits).

The printed document is served by a two-line executable inventory script (#!/bin/sh; exec cat <doc>), mirroring inventoryWrapperText; a control document wraps the same value as {"__ansible_unsafe": ...}.

In noixdev/pulsix-worker:dev (ansible-core 2.21.4), with --network none --read-only, the prescribed limits and --ipc private --shm-size 64m, run ansible-playbook -i <script> play.yml for both inventories.
execution.observed_result: RecordFacts accepted the value (err=nil) and Render emitted it raw under pulsix_facts.os. The full ansible-playbook run printed "host os is debian-42-uid65532": the arithmetic evaluated and the pipe lookup ran `id -u` in the controller process. With the __ansible_unsafe-wrapped control the same task printed the value literally.

remediation.strategy: Mark every agent-reported fact unsafe before it enters the inventory document by reusing ansiblevars.Inert (h.Facts is map[string]any, which Inert handles recursively). Add a regression test asserting that pulsix_facts strings render as {"__ansible_unsafe": ...}. Optionally also refuse '{{', '{%' and '{#' in RecordFacts as defence in depth.

likelihood.reason: Requires control of one monitored, managed host (or its agent key) and a later play that evaluates pulsix_facts, which is the variable's documented purpose. No operator credential is needed.

impact.reason: Command execution in the zone worker's Ansible controller as the run's play identity, a host-to-controller trust crossing. The play identity can read the connection material that run is given for the other hosts in its scope, enabling lateral movement within the organization.

confidence.reason: Every trace line verified in source at b13f3c6. Independently reproduced: the Pulsix half (RecordFacts + Render) in the Go sandbox, and a full ansible-playbook run in the actual worker image with ansible-core 2.21.4, with a positive __ansible_unsafe control. Only the Postgres jsonb merge (verbatim by source) and the setuid play-uid drop were not executed; the uid observed was the image's 65532 rather than the production play uid 65533.

title: Plain inventory value under a field reclassified as secret is masked on reads but left off the claim's redact list
description: SetSchema never rewrites stored values. So after a group or membership field changes from string to secret, the old plain value stays in storage until the next SetVars/Assign. Since backlog 2.21 the read path (groupView/memberView via schema.MaskDeclared) treats that value as secret and returns {$secret:set} to viewers. The claim snapshot still renders the plain value into InventoryDoc for the worker. Renderer.secrets adds a value to the revealed list only when it was a sealed envelope it opened, so Snapshot.Secrets, and therefore workerpb.Job.redact, leaves the plain value out. The worker's redactor uses only Job.redact plus credential parts, so a task that prints the var or returns it in a module result forwards it in clear. Any org viewer (jobs.read) can then read it through the job events API, while the inventory API masks the same value for that viewer.
root_cause: Renderer.secrets (internal/inventory/renderer.go:271-282) decides what to redact by whether the value is sealed: a non-sealed value under a secret-typed field returns early without being appended to revealed. The read path (schema.MaskDeclared) masks every non-empty value under a secret-typed field. The two classifications of the same stored value disagree, and SetSchema (service.go:346-376) deliberately leaves the plain value in storage.
intended_behavior: Every value the system hides from viewers as secret (a non-empty value under a secret-typed field, backlog 2.21 MaskDeclared) is also on the claim's redact list, so run output withholds it the way the inventory read API does. newRedactor's own doc names 'secret inventory vars' as part of that list.

trace.description: An org viewer, the lowest role, reads a job's stored run events.
An admin's string to secret schema change rewrites no stored value, so the plain value stays under the now-secret field.
For a non-sealed value under a secret field, SealedBytes reports !ok and the value is returned as-is without being appended to revealed.
out.Secrets = secretsInDoc(revealed, out.Doc): the plain value is in the doc but missing from Secrets.
redact.add(inv.Secrets...) builds Job.Redact. InventoryDoc (from inv.Doc at line 564) carries the plain value, but the redact list has no entry for it.
The worker redacts only Job.redact entries and credential PrivateKey/Password/Token. runner.go:277 applies this redactor to streamed events.
deps.Jobs.Events returns the stored event payloads, and with them the printed plain value, to the viewer unredacted.

evidence.description: return v, nil inside if !ok: a non-sealed value under a secret field is never appended to revealed.
MaskDeclared masks every non-empty value of a secret-typed field, sealed or not (backlog 2.21).
Comment: a string to secret schema change reseals nothing; only the next SetVars/Assign does.
SetSchema doc: stored values are never rewritten.
groupView applies MaskDeclared, so GetGroup shows {$secret:set} to an inventory.read viewer. members.go:119 does the same for memberships.
The newRedactor doc says the manager's redact list covers 'secret inventory vars'.
PermJobsRead is granted at RoleViewer.

conditions.description: The reader is an org member with jobs.read (viewer or above).
A group or membership field held a non-empty plain string and an admin then changed its type to secret. No SetVars/Assign has resealed that row since.
A run over that scope executes a task (written by an operator or above) that prints the var or returns it in a module result.

execution.attacker_perspective: An org viewer, to whom the inventory API shows the value as {$secret:set}, reads it in clear in a job's run log.
payloads: SetSchema api_token:string; SetVars api_token=plain-token-v15; SetSchema api_token:secret; GetGroup; Snapshot(scope = group webserver)
instructions: Copy the repository to scratch and drop the three DB-backed test files in internal/inventory (concurrency_test.go, renderer_integration_test.go, store_sql_test.go).

Add a test in package inventory_test that reuses the package's own rendererFixture (in-memory fakeStore, testBox): extend webSchema with api_token:string, SetVars it to plain-token-v15, retype it to secret with SetSchema, then call Service.GetGroup and Renderer.Snapshot(scope GroupID = webserver).
Log GetGroup vars, the snapshot doc value and Snapshot.Secrets.
Run go test -count=1 -v -run TestV15PlainUnderSecretFieldRedactList ./internal/inventory/ in the approved Docker sandbox (no network, read-only source, no database).
The claim (queue_sql.go:539-647), worker redaction (redact.go:47-80, runner.go:277) and events route steps are source reads.
execution.observed_result: GetGroup and the SetSchema response returned api_token = {"$secret":"set"}. The stored value stayed "plain-token-v15". The snapshot doc webserver.vars.api_token was "plain-token-v15". Snapshot.Secrets was ["group-secret" "member-secret"], so the plain-under-secret value was not listed (listed = false) while the sealed group and membership secrets were.

remediation.strategy: Make Renderer.secrets use the same rule as MaskDeclared. In the reveal branch, append a non-empty plain string found under a secret-typed field to revealed before returning it. secretsInDoc then scopes it like a sealed value. Add a renderer test asserting the value is in Snapshot.Secrets after a string to secret change. Optionally, have SetSchema reseal plain values under newly secret fields so the transitional state does not exist.

likelihood.reason: Three things must coincide: an admin reclassifies an already-populated string field to secret, nobody re-saves that group or membership's vars before a run, and a playbook task (authored by operator+) prints the var or returns it in a module result.

impact.reason: It exposes one inventory value to org viewers through the run log. Viewers could read that value in clear before the reclassification, so the exposure reaches viewers after the admin designated it secret, including viewers added later. No cross-tenant or role escalation.

confidence.reason: The renderer step was independently reproduced with the package's real Service and Renderer over its own in-memory fakes in the sandbox. The remaining claim, worker-redaction and events-API steps are direct, short source reads at b13f3c6.

title: Host agent can inject forged lines and chat markup into alert notifications via check-result item names
description: A host agent (a compromised managed host, or anyone holding that host's agent mTLS key) chooses the 'item' string of every check result it sends. The manager stores it verbatim, opens alerts on it, and copies it unchanged into notify.AlertItem. Neither the agent ingest contract nor the notification renderer refuses control characters or line breaks. The one-line-per-alert text that the plain-text alert e-mail and the {{ alerts.items }} webhook placeholder both use can therefore carry extra lines the host chooses: forged alert rows naming other hosts, or phishing text and URLs inside a message sent by the instance's trusted Pulsix sender. Chat receivers fed by a body template also get mention or markdown payloads such as '@everyone' or masked links. JSON escaping keeps the webhook body valid JSON, but the receiver still shows \n as a line break. Headers and SMTP framing are not affected: the subject carries only the count and org name, and the body is dot-stuffed.
root_cause: checks.withinContract (internal/checks/samples.go) bounds item only by length (<=512 bytes). The rules, alerts and alertroutes pipeline copies the item unchanged, and notify.alertItemsText (internal/notify/render.go) concatenates it raw into a line-oriented message. Sibling human-visible names (org, channel and group names, rule names) reject unicode.IsControl, but agent-supplied items do not.
intended_behavior: An agent-reported item (a mount point or unit name) should never be able to add lines or formatting to a notification. Refuse items with control characters at ingest, or have alertItemsText escape or replace control characters in every field so each alert stays exactly one line.

trace.description: The agent's CheckResult.item (a proto3 string: any valid UTF-8, including \n) is copied verbatim into checks.Observation.Item from the mTLS-authenticated AgentStream.
The only check on item is len(o.Item) > MaxItemLen (512). Control characters and line breaks are accepted, and RecordObservations stores the item.

The stored tuple, item included, is read back for evaluation. Items without a decision resolve to Watch (internal/items/decide.go:163), so a threshold breach under a seeded rule opens an alert whose subject carries the raw item.
The alert event's Item is copied verbatim into notify.AlertItem for every routed channel. follow_escalate.go:331 does the same for escalations.
what += "/" + it.Item, then fmt.Sprintf at line 228 without escaping, so embedded newlines become extra lines.
The alert text is written into the plain-text e-mail body. The same text feeds the {{ alerts.items }} placeholder (placeholders.go:157-158, 314), where escapedText only JSON-escapes it.

evidence.description: withinContract checks only empty values and length bounds for check_key, item and metric, with no character-class restriction. A sandbox harness (re-run by the Phase 5 verifier, agents/f09-agent-item-unsanitized/artifacts/evidence2.txt) confirmed it returns nil for an item containing \n, \r and ESC.
Each alert line is fmt.Sprintf("%-8s %-20s %-8s %s", ...) built from raw agent-controlled text.
The default placeholder form only JSON-escapes (json.Marshal of fieldText), so newlines and markup survive into the text the receiver displays.
With no matching decision the verdict is Watch, so a newly reported item is evaluated by default.
A sibling control: monitoring group names reject unicode.IsControl, as do notify/validate.go:46 and rules/service.go:198. Agent items do not.
The escalation path also copies Subject.Item verbatim into an AlertItem.

conditions.description: The attacker controls one enrolled host agent (root on a managed host, or holding that host's agent mTLS key).

A rule matches the reported check_key and metric (the seeded 'Disk usage warning/critical' rules match check_key 'disk', metric 'disk.used_pct' for every item), and an alert route sends that host's alerts to an e-mail channel or to a webhook channel whose template uses {{ alerts.items }}.
Impact needs a recipient to read and trust the forged lines or links, or a chat platform to honour the injected mention.

execution.attacker_perspective: The agent on a compromised managed host reports a disk observation (metric disk.used_pct) whose item contains line breaks, a forged alert row for another host and a phishing line, with a value high enough to open an alert.
payloads: body template: {"content": "{{ alerts.items }}"}
Observation{CheckKey:"disk", Metric:"disk.used_pct", Item:"/var\ncrit db-prod-1 opened\r\n@everyone \x1b[31m"}
instructions: In a scratch copy of the source, add a package-internal test in internal/notify that builds an EventAlertBatch with the AlertItem payload above, which is the shape Follower.decide produces from an alert whose subject item the agent supplied.
Call renderEmail(ev), alertItemsText, checkBodyTemplate(template, true) and renderWebhookBody(template, ev), then print the results and decode the webhook JSON.
Add a package-internal test in internal/checks that calls withinContract on the Observation payload above.
Run both with go test -run in the network-less, read-only Docker sandbox. Other *_test.go files in those two packages are moved aside in the scratch copy so the packages compile without testdb.
execution.observed_result: renderEmail produced a four-line body from one alert item: 'warn web-7 opened disk//var', a forged 'crit db-prod-1 opened disk/ disk.used_pct' row for another host, a blank line, and 'ACTION REQUIRED: re-authenticate at https://attacker.invalid/login @everyone disk.used_pct'. alertItemsText returned 4 lines for 1 item. checkBodyTemplate accepted the template (nil). renderWebhookBody returned valid JSON whose decoded content held the same forged lines and the @everyone mention. withinContract returned nil for an item with \n, \r and ESC. The DB-backed steps (store, rules evaluation, alert opening, follower) were traced from source only.

remediation.strategy: Enforce at both ends. At ingest, refuse any check_key, item or metric that contains a unicode control character, mirroring the sibling name validators. In notify.alertItemsText, also neutralise control characters in every field so a stored legacy row cannot break the one-line-per-alert format. Regression tests: an item containing \n or \r is refused by RecordObservations, and alertItemsText output has exactly len(items)-1 newlines.

likelihood.reason: It needs control of an enrolled host agent (root on a managed host) and an alert route to an e-mail channel or a templated chat channel.

impact.reason: Content spoofing and phishing text inside trusted alert notifications, plus mention or markup injection in chat. There is no header or SMTP injection, code execution, data disclosure or cross-tenant effect, and a host can already lie about its own metrics.

confidence.reason: Both ends were observed locally in the sandbox (twice, independently): the ingest contract accepts control characters, and the renderer emits the injected lines. The DB-backed middle (storage, rules evaluation, alert creation, follower) is traced from source only, and no filter was found on it.

title: Pinned jump host's key is not enforced when its route also contains an unpinned password-only or credential-less jump host
description: The worker enforces a pinned bastion's host key only through a per-bastion ssh_config alias block (Host pulsix-jump-<id>, HostKeyAlias pulsix-jump-<id>, StrictHostKeyChecking yes). mergeInventory gives up the alias rewrite for the whole chain as soon as any hop has no private key and is itself unpinned. The raw 'ProxyJump=user@addr:port,...' value then stays as it was. The pinned hop is dialed by its real address, which matches only the catch-all 'Host *' block (StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new) against the run's fresh known_hosts, where the pin is stored only under the unused alias. The run reports no error. A network attacker in front of the pinned bastion is accepted with any host key, can finish authentication (observed with 'none'), and receives the tunnel (direct-tcpip) requests for the rest of the route. The defect affects template and ad-hoc runs, and also the bootstrap, rotate_key and revoke_key system jobs, because they reach the same mergeInventory through oneHostInventory/synthRunJob. A pinned target host is still verified end to end through the tunnel. For unpinned later hops and an unpinned target, however, the connection passes through the attacker. Capture of later password prompts or of the target's credential was not demonstrated.
root_cause: The fail-closed guard in mergeInventory (internal/worker/runner/inventory.go:103) checks only whether the hop that cannot be scripted is pinned (bastionPins[bastionID]). When that hop is unpinned, lines 106-107 set blocks=nil and break. This throws away the strict block already built for an earlier pinned hop and never looks at pinned hops later in the chain. Line 113 then skips the host, leaving the raw chain. The misaligned-chain path (line 86) and the failed-rewrite path (line 116) also 'continue' without checking pins. pinBastions (line 406) still writes the pinned key under 'pulsix-jump-<id>', but nothing dials that alias. sshConfigText's catch-all (sshconfig.go:179, knownHostsDefaults at sshconfig.go:160) applies accept-new to the raw hop address.
intended_behavior: When a route dials a pinned bastion, that hop must be checked strictly against its pinned key. If the worker cannot alias the chain (a hop that cannot be scripted anywhere in the chain, a misaligned chain, or a failed rewrite) and the route contains ANY pinned bastion, the run must fail closed. The existing comment at inventory.go:36-39 already states this intent: 'an unaliasable hop could never enforce its pin'.

trace.description: The claim ships each route's bastion ids with aligned bastion credential ids: an empty string for a credential-less bastion, and Secret JSON without private_key for a password credential. Org operators/admins configure the route; the lower-trust actor is the network peer the worker later dials.
The route's pinned bastions ship as bastion_host_keys (fingerprint) and bastion_known_hosts (full key), keyed by bastion id.
mergeInventory is called with the claim's connections, credentials and bastion pins. Bootstrap, rotate_key and revoke_key reach it too, through oneHostInventory and synthRunJob.

For a hop without a private key, only that hop's own pin is checked. An unpinned password-only or credential-less hop sets blocks=nil and breaks (lines 106-107), which drops the pinned hop's strict block or never reaches a later pinned hop.
With blocks nil the host is skipped. ansible_ssh_common_args keeps the raw 'ProxyJump=user@addr:port,...' chain, and no error is returned.
The pinned key is written to the run's known_hosts only under 'pulsix-jump-<id>', an alias the raw chain never uses.

The only remaining block is 'Host *' with knownHostsDefaults (sshconfig.go:160: StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new). The ProxyJump child ssh reads this file (via -F from sshArgs, layout.go:93), matches the raw hop address against that block, and accepts and records whatever key an impostor presents.

evidence.description: The guard checks bastionPins[bastionID] only for the hop that cannot be scripted. The else path (blocks = nil; break at lines 106-107) discards every other hop's pin.
A misaligned chain does 'continue' without checking bastion pins. This shares the root cause; it was not demonstrated.
A chain that cannot be rewritten does 'continue' without checking bastion pins. This shares the root cause; it was not demonstrated.
The raw hop address resolves to the catch-all 'Host *' block with accept-new.
The existing regression test covers only a pinned hop that is itself password-only. No test covers a pinned key hop next to an unpinned password-only or credential-less hop.
System jobs build the same aligned bastion credential ids and reuse mergeInventory, so bootstrap, rotate_key and revoke_key have the same defect.

A bastion credential may be either an SSH key or an SSH password, or the bastion may have none, and pins are set per bastion. A route that mixes a pinned key hop with an unpinned password-only hop is therefore a valid configuration; nothing on the manager side refuses it.

conditions.description: An organization route contains at least one bastion pinned with a full key AND at least one unpinned bastion whose credential is password-only or absent, in either order. The route can come from a host, group or zone bastion setting, or from a bastion's via-chain.
The attacker can intercept or redirect the worker's TCP connection to the pinned bastion's address. This is exactly the threat the bastion pin exists to stop.
The attacker needs no Pulsix privilege. Org operators/admins configure the route in the normal way, and any run, ad-hoc command, bootstrap, rotation or revocation over it triggers the dial.

execution.attacker_perspective: A network-positioned attacker impersonates a jump host the organization has pinned, against a worker dialing a route that also includes an unpinned jump host with a password credential or no credential.
payloads: Claim (workerpb.Job): connections {"web1": {host_id:u1, credential_id:cHOST, bastions:[bPIN,bPW|bNONE], bastion_credential_ids:[cKEY,cPW|""]}}, inventory hostvar ansible_ssh_common_args '-o ProxyJump=jump@127.0.0.1:2201,ops@10.0.0.8:22', credentials cKEY={private_key}, cPW={password}, bastion_host_keys {bPIN: SHA256 of a generated ed25519 key}, bastion_known_hosts {bPIN: that key}
Loopback impostor on 127.0.0.1:2201: x/crypto/ssh server with a freshly generated ed25519 host key (not the pin), NoClientAuth, rejecting every channel

ssh -v -F <run ssh_config> -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o UserKnownHostsFile=<run known_hosts> -o GlobalKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 -o ProxyJump=jump@127.0.0.1:2201,ops@10.0.0.8:22 -l root 10.0.0.10 true
instructions: Copy the repository into scratch. Add the harness internal/worker/runner/zz_v18_pins_test.go, which calls the real (&Runner{}).materializeInventory with the claim above for these cases: pinned hop first + password hop, pinned hop first + credential-less hop, pinned hop second + password hop, a pinned-only control, and a pinned password-only control. Add the loopback impostor internal/zzv18/fakesshd (sources in agents/v18-ssh-pins/artifacts/evidence3.txt).

In the approved golang:1.27.1-alpine sandbox (network none, read-only source), run: go test -count=1 -v -run TestV18MixedChainPin ./internal/worker/runner/ (agents/v18-ssh-pins/artifacts/evidence.txt). Then build the impostor.

In noixdev/pulsix-worker:dev (--network none --read-only, OpenSSH_10.0p2), start the impostor on 127.0.0.1:2201. Dial the target with the ansible-shaped ssh command, using each case's rendered ssh_config, known_hosts and pulsix_ssh_common_args (agents/v18-ssh-pins/artifacts/evidence2.txt).
execution.observed_result: Mixed chains (pinned first or second, with a password or credential-less hop): materializeInventory err=<nil>. The written ssh_config contains only 'Host * / StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new'. pulsix_ssh_common_args keeps the raw '-o ProxyJump=jump@127.0.0.1:2201,ops@10.0.0.8:22'. known_hosts has the pin only as 'pulsix-jump-bPIN ...'. OpenSSH in the worker image printed: "Warning: Permanently added '[127.0.0.1]:2201' (ED25519)" and 'Authenticated to 127.0.0.1 ([127.0.0.1]:2201) using "none"'. The impostor logged: 'client authenticated as "jump"' and 'client opened channel direct-tcpip'. Controls: the pinned-only route rendered the strict alias block and ssh failed with 'Host key for pulsix-jump-bpin has changed ... Host key verification failed.' before authenticating. The pinned password-only hop failed the merge closed.

remediation.strategy: In mergeInventory, fail the merge closed whenever a route that dials ANY pinned bastion cannot be fully aliased: a hop that cannot be scripted anywhere in the chain, a chain that does not match the claim, or a failed rewrite. Do not check only the pin of the hop that cannot be scripted. Effective args without any ProxyJump can still pass through, since they dial no bastion. Add regression tests, all expecting an error: a pinned key hop plus an unpinned password-only hop in both orders, a pinned key hop plus a credential-less hop, and a misaligned chain containing a pinned bastion.

likelihood.reason: Needs a specific but supported configuration (a pinned key bastion and an unpinned bastion with a password credential or none, on the same route) plus an attacker with network position in front of the pinned bastion. On the raw chain the pinned hop's own key file is not referenced either (no IdentityFile for the raw address), so such routes generally fail legitimate authentication. Operators are therefore likely to notice and fix the route, although every retry or scheduled run dials again in the meantime.

impact.reason: Silently defeats the host-key pin, the bastion's only protection against impersonation. The impostor is accepted and recorded, authenticates the worker, and controls the tunnel to later hops and to an unpinned target (observed up to the direct-tcpip request). A pinned target is still verified end to end. Capture of credentials through later hops or the target was not demonstrated.

confidence.reason: Independent reproduction with my own harness through the real Runner.materializeInventory (written files, not only the helpers), for both hop orders and for both password and credential-less hops. The real worker-image OpenSSH client against a loopback impostor accepted the wrong key, while the pinned-only control failed closed. The source trace from claim build to ssh_config was re-checked line by line at b13f3c6.

title: Base64 redaction only matches a secret at a 3-byte-aligned offset, so slurped files leak it
description: Backlog 2.48 added base64 spellings to the worker's redactor because slurp returns file contents base64-encoded. base64Spellings encodes only the secret by itself. When the secret sits inside a larger encoded buffer at a byte offset that is 1 or 2 mod 3, as with a typical config line like 'pwd=<secret>', the encoded content contains none of the listed spellings. eventPayload forwards the module result unredacted, the manager stores it as received, and an org viewer (jobs.read) reads it from the job events API and base64-decodes the secret.
root_cause: Base64 output depends on where the secret falls within the encoded buffer's 3-byte groups. base64Spellings lists only the encodings of the whole value starting on a group boundary. It lists no stable inner core for offsets 1 and 2 mod 3. Even at offset 0, the last character of the unpadded spelling of a value whose length is not a multiple of 3 depends on the byte that follows the secret.
intended_behavior: A secret that a slurp or b64encode result carries is replaced before the event leaves the worker (internal/worker/runner/redact.go base64Spellings doc comment; backlog 2.48 says a secret read out of a file and printed is now covered).

trace.description: The claim names secret inventory vars (and, just above, every opened credential) on Job.redact. This is the only source of values the worker redacts.
Only the four whole-value encodings of v are added to the redact set.
event_data.res (for example slurp's content field) is redacted by literal substring match only.
The payload is stored as received. normalizePayload only reshapes invalid JSON.
Gated by PermJobsRead (viewer). toJobEventDTO returns the stored payload, so a viewer reads res.content and base64-decodes the secret.

evidence.description: The encoders run over []byte(v) alone. There is no offset-shifted or trimmed-core variant.
The res key of event_data is always forwarded, so slurp's content reaches the event whatever the verbosity.
Every mapped ansible event goes to the sink through red.eventPayload. No other redaction pass runs on the worker or the manager.
jobs.read is granted to the viewer role, which is below the operator+ principals that the spec accepts can obtain job credentials.

conditions.description: Org viewer (jobs.read) reading a run's events.

A legitimate task, written by an operator or above, base64-encodes data that embeds a claim secret without no_log. Examples are slurp of a config file that holds a secret inventory var or credential, or b64encode of a templated string.
The secret's byte offset in the encoded buffer is 1 or 2 mod 3, which covers about two thirds of placements.

execution.attacker_perspective: An org viewer reads the events of a run whose task slurped a config file embedding a secret var.
payloads: secret on Job.redact: s3cr3tPassw0rd
slurped file bytes: pwd=s3cr3tPassw0rd\n -> res.content cHdkPXMzY3IzdFBhc3N3MHJkCg==
instructions: In a scratch copy of the repo, add a package-internal test in internal/worker/runner that builds newRedactor(&workerpb.Job{Redact: []string{secret}}).

For each prefix ("", "a", "ab", "abc", "pwd=", "db_pass=", "password: "), build a runner_on_ok event whose event_data.res is a slurp result {content: base64(prefix+secret+"\n"), encoding: base64}. Pass it through r.eventPayload, then decode the forwarded res.content.
Run go test -run TestV16Base64Alignment ./internal/worker/runner/ in the approved network-less, read-only Docker sandbox.
execution.observed_result: Through the real eventPayload, offsets 0 and 3 were redacted. Offsets 1, 2, 4, 8 and 10 were forwarded unchanged. For example, offset 4 forwarded cHdkPXMzY3IzdFBhc3N3MHJkCg==, and the decoded content contained s3cr3tPassw0rd (agents/v16-job-output/artifacts/evidence.txt).

remediation.strategy: In base64Spellings, also list the alignment-independent core of the secret for each offset class: the unpadded std and URL encoding of v[skip:] trimmed to whole 3-byte groups, for skip 0, 1 and 2, with a minimum core length so short cores cannot shred output. This also covers the tail-character dependence at offset 0. Add a regression test over offsets 0..5 with differing following bytes.

likelihood.reason: It requires a legitimate task that base64-encodes a buffer embedding a claim secret without no_log, such as slurp of a config file, and a misaligned offset, which happens about two thirds of the time. The viewer cannot cause the task.

impact.reason: A viewer recovers a secret var or credential value that redaction promised to hide from them. The leak is limited to the values the task happened to encode.

confidence.reason: This is deterministic encoding behavior. It was reproduced independently in the sandbox through the real eventPayload at offsets 0 through 4, 8 and 10, and the source trace to the viewer-readable events endpoint was verified line by line.

title: Run-output redaction misses secrets that contain a quote or backslash together with &, < or > in ansible's display text
description: The worker's redactor replaces each claim secret's raw value and its Go json.Marshal spelling. ansible-core's result display (default callback, result_format json) serializes module results with Python json.dumps(ensure_ascii=False), which escapes " and \ but leaves &, < and > literal. Go's encoder HTML-escapes those three (\u0026, \u003c, \u003e). So for a secret that has a JSON-escaped character and one of &, < or >, neither listed spelling appears in the display stdout. The secret is forwarded unredacted in the event's stdout field, stored as-is in job_events, and shown to any org member with jobs.read (viewer) through the events API, the SSE stream and the run view's EventLog. The structured event_data.res copy of the same value is redacted, so the gap is only the display text. Evidence from the audit run: a real runner_on_ok event captured from the worker image (ansible-runner 2.4.3 / ansible-core 2.21.4, network none) carries stdout `"db_password": "Tr&ub4dor\"3x"`, so & is literal and " is escaped; feeding that exact line through the real Runner.streamEvents with Redact=[Tr&ub4dor"3x, Troub4dor"3x] forwarded stdout that still contained the secret, while the control secret without & was redacted and res.db_password was [redacted] in both.
root_cause: newRedactor (internal/worker/runner/redact.go:54-57) derives the only escaped spelling with json.Marshal, whose default HTML escaping does not match the escaping of the Python producer of ansible's display text. text() does literal substring replacement, so a spelling mismatch means the secret is not redacted.
intended_behavior: internal/jobs/redact.go (package comment) says viewers with jobs.read must never see a credential, secret extra var or secret inventory var that a task printed. internal/worker/runner/redact.go:43-44 says each value is also redacted in its JSON-escaped spelling because display text shows module results as JSON. That spelling has to match what ansible actually emits.

trace.description: On claim, every opened credential (and, on the next line, inventory secrets) goes onto workerpb.Job.redact. This is where the protected secret enters the run. The lower-trust reader is the viewer at the sink.
The only escaped spelling is built with json.Marshal, which HTML-escapes & < >. The set holds the raw value, the Go-escaped value and base64 forms, but not the Python json.dumps form.
Each ansible-runner --json event line with a state is forwarded as red.eventPayload(ev).
The display stdout (ansible's json.dumps spelling of the result) only goes through text(), which replaces the listed literals. None of them match.
The manager stores the payload as received, because normalizePayload passes valid JSON through unchanged, and publishes it to SSE subscribers.
requireOrg(PermJobsRead) lets a viewer read the stored payload, including the unredacted stdout. The SSE route (job_sse.go:40) has the same gate.

evidence.description: esc := string(b[1 : len(b)-1]) from json.Marshal is the only escaped spelling added.
text() does literal strings.ReplaceAll on the listed values only.
PermJobsRead is granted to RoleViewer.
The run view renders payload.stdout verbatim.

conditions.description: The reader needs only the viewer role (jobs.read) in the organization that ran the job.
The secret has at least one JSON-escaped character (", \ or a control character, e.g. a newline in a multi-line value) AND at least one of &, < or >.

A task's display output includes the value, e.g. debug of the var, a module result echoing it, or a failed command's output in the JSON result. This is the accidental print that redaction exists to catch.
The default ansible result_format json applies. The worker-generated ansible.cfg (layout.go ansibleCfgText) does not change it.

execution.attacker_perspective: An org viewer with jobs.read opens the run log, or calls the events/SSE API, for a job whose task printed a secret containing such characters.
payloads: secret on the claim redact list: Tr&ub4dor"3x (control: Troub4dor"3x)
playbook task: ansible.builtin.debug: var=db_password with extravars {"db_password": "Tr&ub4dor\"3x"}
instructions: In the worker image noixdev/pulsix-worker:dev (network none, read-only, tmpfs-only writes), run ansible-runner run on a local-connection playbook with two debug tasks printing db_password=Tr&ub4dor"3x and ctrl_password=Troub4dor"3x. Capture the runner_on_ok job_event lines.

Copy the repository into scratch and add a package-internal test in internal/worker/runner. It feeds those exact lines to (&Runner{}).streamEvents with newRedactor(&workerpb.Job{Redact: []string{`Tr&ub4dor"3x`, `Troub4dor"3x`}}), then decodes each forwarded payload's stdout.
Run go test -run TestV17RealAnsibleDisplayRedaction ./internal/worker/runner/ in the network-less, read-only golang sandbox.
execution.observed_result: ansible's display stdout was ok: [localhost] => {\r\n    "db_password": "Tr&ub4dor\"3x"\r\n}. After streamEvents, the forwarded payload's stdout still read "db_password": "Tr&ub4dor\"3x" (contains secret=true), while event_data.res.db_password was [redacted]. The control secret Troub4dor"3x was [redacted] in both stdout and res. Storage and API exposure are source-verified only, because the DB-backed packages cannot run in the sandbox. Recorded in the v17-job-output run artifacts: evidence2.txt line 4 is the real ansible-runner 2.4.3 / ansible-core 2.21.4 runner_on_ok event, and evidence.txt lines 6 and 11 are the redaction outcome for the control secret and the & secret.

remediation.strategy: Add the Python json.dumps(ensure_ascii=False) spelling next to the Go one. Escape only ", \ and control characters, and leave &, <, >, U+2028/U+2029 and non-ASCII literal. A plain SetEscapeHTML(false) encoder still differs on U+2028/U+2029 and invalid UTF-8, so a hand-written escaper is the exact match. Keep the existing json.Marshal spelling. Add a regression test that feeds a recorded ansible-runner event with a secret mixing "/\ with &/</>.

likelihood.reason: It needs a secret with both character classes (common in generated passwords, but not universal) and a task that prints it.
