impact.reason: The lowest org role reads a cleartext managed-host credential or secret var that the product explicitly withholds from viewers.

confidence.reason: The display spelling comes from real ansible-core 2.21.4 / ansible-runner 2.4.3 output in the worker image, and that output went through the real Go streamEvents/redactor path. The json.dumps(ensure_ascii=False) call was read in the image's callback source. Manager storage and API exposure are source-only but straightforward: valid JSON is stored verbatim behind a jobs.read gate.

title: Worker-uid writes and chmods follow paths in a work dir the play group can already modify
description: With PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID set, newWorkDir makes the run's work dir mode 02770, group 65532, before any run file is written (workdir.go:44). The play uid has 65532 as its primary gid and the dir has no sticky bit, so any play-uid process can create, rename or replace entries in it. The worker then operates by path as its own uid: writeTextFile/writeSecretFile call os.MkdirAll and os.WriteFile (follow a pre-planted symlink, layout.go:67,70); ShareWorkDir checks the readdir d_type for symlinks then calls lstat and os.Chmod by path and descends with WalkDir (share.go:40-56). Local checks: (1) Go sandbox - a planted symlink at work/ssh_config sent writeTextFile's content into a dummy outside file, and a goroutine flipping a work-dir subdir to a symlink pointing at a dummy 0700 dir won the ShareWorkDir race at iteration 399, taking the outside dir to 2770 and its dummy key to 0660 (evidence.txt). (2) Shipped worker image - a play started via the setuid helper SIGKILLed its own supervisor (same uid 65533); a setsid'd uid-65533 child then survived the run, reparented to PID 1, and another uid's /proc/<pid>/cmdline was readable (evidence2.txt). The worker backstop signals only the original pgid (runner.go:543,639), not a setsid'd process. (3) Source - an SSH-remote repo-backed job embeds <workDir>/home/.ssh/known_hosts (and -i <workDir>/gitkeys/<id>) in git's ssh argv during materializePlaybook, before materializeInventory and ShareWorkDir (gitrepo.go:135,158,182; runner.go:164-180), leaking the random work-dir name via /proc cmdline; for inline/adhoc jobs no source-visible discovery channel exists (data dir 0710, random MkdirTemp suffix). Attacker: an operator+ org member whose arbitrary play-uid code is accepted by design. Boundary crossed: the play-uid separation protecting the worker's identity dir and data dir. Result: worker-uid overwrite/truncation and a wide chmod of worker-owned paths. The integrated cross-uid chain against a live worker loop was not executed.
claimed_root_cause: The worker materializes and shares run files with path-based, symlink-following operations (os.MkdirAll, os.WriteFile, lstat-then-os.Chmod by name, WalkDir descent) inside a directory that is group-writable by the play from the moment it is created, with no sticky bit. Play-uid processes are contained only by a per-run supervisor running as the play's own uid, which the play can kill, so a play-uid process can survive into later jobs and substitute entries while the worker materializes them.

trace.description: With PlayUID set the setuid helper execs the play supervisor as the play uid. The play (operator-supplied code) can SIGKILL its supervisor and leave a setsid'd play-uid process running after the job, observed in the shipped image (evidence2.txt).
The next job's work dir is chmodded to 02770 (group 65532 = play's primary gid, no sticky bit) before any run file is written, so play-uid processes can create, rename or replace any entry in it.

For an SSH-remote repo-backed job, GIT_SSH_COMMAND carries UserKnownHostsFile=<workDir>/home/.ssh/known_hosts (and -i <workDir>/gitkeys/<id> at line 158); git's ssh child exposes the work dir path via /proc cmdline before materializeInventory and ShareWorkDir run.

Run files are written by path with os.WriteFile (O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, follows a pre-planted symlink) after os.MkdirAll (line 67) accepts a symlinked parent. Demonstrated: a dummy outside file was overwritten (evidence.txt).
ShareWorkDir runs on the work dir as the worker uid after all run files are materialized and before the play spawns.

os.Chmod(path) follows a symlink swapped in after the readdir d_type check (line 40), and WalkDir descends through it. Demonstrated: a dummy outside dir went 0700 to 2770 and its dummy key 0600 to 0660 (evidence.txt).

evidence.description: The symlink skip relies on the readdir d_type, taken before d.Info() (lstat, line 43) and os.Chmod by path (line 56); nothing is fd-relative or O_NOFOLLOW.
os.MkdirAll and os.WriteFile by path, without O_NOFOLLOW or O_EXCL, inside the group-writable work dir.
Group write (02770, no sticky bit) is granted at creation, before materialization; fs.protected_symlinks applies only to sticky world-writable dirs, so it does not constrain these follows.
The worker backstop SIGKILL goes only to the run's original pgid (signalGroup, line 543), so a setsid'd play-uid descendant of a killed supervisor is not reached.

The run's known_hosts path under the work dir is created and embedded in the ssh argv for SSH-remote repo fetches before inventory/config materialization and ShareWorkDir, leaking the random work-dir name via /proc/<pid>/cmdline.
The data dir is 0710 (traverse, no list) and MkdirTemp uses a random suffix (workdir.go:39), so for jobs without a git ssh step no discovery channel is source-visible.
The design states the supervisor runs as the play uid, the same uid as everything below it; a hostile play killing its supervisor is not addressed.

blockers: The integrated cross-uid chain was not executed: a real worker loop needs a Postgres-backed manager, an enrolled worker and an SSH git remote for the repo-backed job that leaks the work-dir name, all of which the approved sandbox forbids (no network, no database). Only the components were observed independently: the sink race and symlink-following write in the single-uid Go sandbox, and play-uid survival past its run in the worker image.

Whether a surviving play-uid process can read worker children's /proc/<pid>/cmdline in a deployment depends on the /proc mount options (hidepid) of the deployed container; it was readable cross-uid in the local docker sandbox, but that is a deployment fact.

Whether the identity key becomes readable after the chmod depends on the identity files' group and ownership (data-dir identity is 65532:65532; a bind-mounted /etc/pulsix-worker bundle may differ); the file-level-symlink variant that would chmod a target to 0777 regardless was not observed.

validation_plan.local: On a disposable worker container (noixdev/pulsix-worker:dev, PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID=65533) enrolled to a local dev manager with a dummy org and a local SSH git remote on an isolated docker network, dummy data only: (1) run an inline job whose play double-forks a setsid'd watcher and then SIGKILLs its supervisor; (2) the watcher polls /proc/*/cmdline for 'UserKnownHostsFile=.../job-', then on a hit polls stat of the discovered work dir until the worker starts materializing, and rename-swaps a later-sorted worker-owned subdir (e.g. project or vault) with a symlink to the identity dir; (3) run a repo-backed SSH job to drive the next materialization; (4) stop the moment the identity dir or key mode changes, observed by stat from outside the container. Never read or use the key; restore modes and destroy the container afterward.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-run read-only check on a dummy worker: read the container's /proc mount options (grep ' /proc ' /proc/mounts) for hidepid; record whether PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID is set and which job kinds use SSH-remote repos; after a completed job, list any uid-65533 processes still running to confirm whether a play process can outlive its job in that image.

title: Repo requirements.yml can make the worker-uid galaxy install write outside the per-repo .galaxy directory
description: The sync_repo job runs ansible-galaxy as the worker uid against a requirements.yml taken from the repository, without restricting role names. A role name containing '../' makes ansible-core 2.21.4 extract a repo-supplied tarball outside the -p .galaxy directory into a sibling path (e.g. another repo's cache dir), and a later fetchGit reuses any existing .git there. The traversal is a real ansible-galaxy behaviour, but the write stays inside a single organization's own worker cache, the operation is a worker-uid sync step by design, and the only actor who controls requirements.yml is operator+, so no protected boundary is crossed.
claimed_root_cause: installRequirements (internal/worker/sync.go) gives the repository's requirements.yml to ansible-galaxy as the worker uid with no check of role name or src, and relies on galaxy to keep installs under -p. fetchGit (internal/worker/runner/gitrepo.go) treats any existing <cache>/<org>/<repo>/.git as a clone it made itself.

trace.description: sync_repo job claimed. The repository is fetched and its requirements.yml is located.
Repo-controlled requirements.yml is selected from the clone.
ansible-galaxy install -r <requirements> -p <cache>/<org>/<repo>.galaxy runs as the worker uid with the clone as cwd. Role name and src are not restricted.
An existing .git at another repo's cache path is reused for git fetch/reset without checking who created it.

evidence.description: The galaxy invocation uses only -r and -p, with no role allowlist and no isolation; confirmed in source and reproduced on noixdev/pulsix-worker:dev (ansible-core 2.21.4): a role name '../<id>' with a local tarball src extracts into <cache>/<org>/<id>, outside the .galaxy path, as uid 65532 (agents/v09-repo-sync/artifacts/evidence.txt).
Clone-vs-fetch is decided only by whether .git exists; a pre-placed .git is reused.
USER 65532:65532 — the worker process (and so the sync job) runs as uid 65532.
workers.org_id NOT NULL with a composite FK to zones(org_id,id): a worker is enrolled for one zone of one organization, so its cache serves only that org.
Spec §14: operators+ can run arbitrary code on the org's workers by design, reaching the org's repository cache and the worker's own client certificate and key — explicitly NOT a finding.
Play-uid separation exists to stop a PLAY task (localhost) from reading the worker cert/key; it is not a boundary over the worker-uid repo sync / galaxy install.

reason: The source-visible behaviour in the trace is accurate and the galaxy role-name traversal is genuinely exploitable in the shipped image — I reproduced it in the approved sandbox on noixdev/pulsix-worker:dev (ansible-core 2.21.4, uid 65532): a requirements.yml role with name '../<repoB-id>' and a local tarball src is extracted by ansible-galaxy into <cache>/<org>/<repoB-id> (a sibling of the -p .galaxy path), creating a worker-owned .git tree that fetchGit (gitrepo.go:220) would later reuse. ansible-core's only guard (is_subpath in galaxy/role.py:386) checks tar MEMBER paths against the archive dir, never the role name / self.path, so -p is not an actual containment boundary. However, this is not a vulnerability because no protected trust boundary is crossed: (1) The galaxy install of requirements.yml runs as the WORKER uid by design — architecture §4 lists it as a worker sink and sync.go documents it, and spec §14 explicitly lists 'the repository cache of its organization' and 'the worker's own client certificate and key' among what operator-controlled code on the org's worker legitimately reaches. The candidate's central claim — 'worker-uid influence by content that otherwise only reaches the play uid' — is therefore misattributed: requirements.yml is repo content processed as the worker uid during sync, not play-uid content. Play-uid separation (spec 2026-10-26) protects the worker cert/key from a PLAY task running as localhost, a different operation, and is a within-org hardening that 'narrows only what one trust domain's own playbook can do to its own worker.' (2) The only actor who controls requirements.yml is operator+ (repos.write = RoleOperator, roles.go:101), for whom spec §14 concedes arbitrary code execution on the org's worker and access to the org's repo cache and worker identity — stated to be NOT a finding. The traversal grants this actor nothing beyond powers already conceded; anyone able to queue a sync_repo job can equally queue jobs.run/playbook code on the same worker. (3) There is no cross-tenant reach: a worker is enrolled for one zone of one organization (00017_workers.sql: org_id NOT NULL + composite zone FK; cert org+zone SAN), the manager hands it only that org's jobs, and each org runs its own worker with its own DataDir. A '../../<otherOrg>/<repo>' name would create a directory on THIS org's worker filesystem, but another org's sync runs on its own separate worker and never reads it. The downstream 'git fetch/reset on a pre-placed .git' (candidate blocker 2) is moot: even full worker-uid code execution via a poisoned .git/config is already conceded to operators and confined to one org's worker. The sandbox reproduction resolves the hunter's primary blocker (galaxy behaviour) in favour of the behaviour being real, while source settles the security question against the finding, so the correct state is rejected rather than needs_validation. (Defence-in-depth note, not a finding: pulsix could still reject role names containing '/' or '..' before invoking ansible-galaxy to keep installs provably inside .galaxy.)

title: Anonymous access to huma's default /schemas/{name} route bypasses the MFA gate on the API description
description: The manager deliberately gates /api/explorer and /api/openapi* behind an MFA-complete session because, unauthenticated, they "hand any caller the full shape of the API" (internal/api/api.go:451-459). api.New builds the huma API from huma.DefaultConfig, which in huma v2.39.1 also sets SchemasPath="/schemas" and registers GET /schemas/{schema} on the root chi router. That path is outside /api, so staticSessionSkip never resolves the session and requireMFAForExplorer never checks it. Any anonymous caller can fetch the JSON Schema of every registered DTO by name (e.g. CredentialDTO, HostDTO). The route is self-advertising: every huma error response, including an anonymous 401, carries Link: </schemas/ErrorModel.json>; rel="describedBy" and a $schema field, and $ref links inside schemas chain to further /schemas/*.json documents. The project's own backlog row 1.29 dropped hardening of /schemas/* on the belief that "no such route exists", which the reproduction disproves. Only the API's shape (field names, types, enums) is disclosed: no tenant data, credentials or secrets, and no state change.
root_cause: internal/api/api.go:433 starts from huma.DefaultConfig, overrides only OpenAPIPath (/api/openapi) and DocsPath (""), and keeps SchemasPath="/schemas". humachi.New (api.go:437) therefore mounts GET /schemas/{schema} outside the /api subtree. requireMFAForExplorer (api.go:460-462) gates only the exact path /api/explorer and the /api/openapi prefix, and skipsSessionLookup (session_skip.go:46-47) skips the session for every non-/api path, so this sibling route describing the same API is served to anyone.
intended_behavior: Every route that discloses the API's machine-readable description is reachable only with an MFA-complete session, the same as /api/openapi*, or does not exist.

trace.description: humachi.New(r, cfg) registers huma's built-in GET /schemas/{schema} handler on the root chi router (cfg.SchemasPath is huma's default "/schemas"), reachable by any unauthenticated HTTP client of the manager listener.
Returns true for any path not starting with /api, so staticSessionSkip (mounted at api.go:380) bypasses the session middleware for /schemas/*; no principal is ever attached.

The MFA gate (mounted at api.go:403) matches only /api/explorer and the /api/openapi prefix, so /schemas/{name}.json passes straight through to huma's schema handler and a 200 JSON Schema is returned to the anonymous caller.

evidence.description: cfg := huma.DefaultConfig("Pulsix API", "0.1.0"); huma v2.39.1 defaults.go sets SchemasPath "/schemas" and api.go:613-616 registers GET SchemasPath+"/{schema}" when it is non-empty.
Only DocsPath is cleared (and OpenAPIPath moved under /api at line 434); SchemasPath is never overridden.
Design comment: the explorer and OpenAPI spec must not, unauthenticated, hand any caller the full shape of the API; the schemas route violates that intent.
Backlog 1.29 drops the /schemas/* hardening half with "no such route exists", showing the route is unintended and unaccounted for.

conditions.description: None. Any network client that can reach the manager's HTTP listener (published on 8080 / behind the reverse proxy in the compose stack).

The caller needs a schema name; ErrorModel is advertised in the Link header of any anonymous huma error, DTO names follow a guessable *DTO/*Body pattern, and $ref links chain from a known name to related schemas.

title: Job log SSE stream keeps delivering after membership removal, token revocation or user deactivation
description: GET /api/v1/orgs/{org}/jobs/{id}/stream authorizes the caller once, with requireOrg(jobs.read), and then returns a huma StreamResponse whose writeJobStream loop forwards every broker log event and status change for that one job until the job reaches a terminal status, the subscription closes, a write fails, or the client disconnects. The loop never re-checks the principal. A member who opened the stream and is then removed from the org, has the pxt_ token they used revoked, or is deactivated by an instance admin (DeactivateUser revokes sessions and tokens and documents that this ends access 'immediately') keeps receiving that run's live play output. No in-process revocation hook cancels open requests, no chi Timeout middleware wraps the route, and the manager's http.Server sets only ReadHeaderTimeout, so the stale stream lasts as long as the run. The exposure is limited to the one job the principal was authorized to read when the stream opened; the principal cannot open new streams or reach other jobs after revocation (requireOrg re-reads membership and the token per request).
claimed_root_cause: writeJobStream (internal/api/job_sse.go) treats the one-time requireOrg decision made when the request starts as valid for the whole stream. Its 500 ms ticker re-reads only the job row through the org-scoped request context (the RLS scope binds the org, not the principal), never the session, the token or the membership, and nothing outside the loop cancels the request when access is revoked.

trace.description: requireOrg(ctx, deps, in.Org, tenancy.PermJobsRead) authorizes the session or bearer principal (membership via MembershipOf, token capped with tenancy.Lower) once, when the request starts.
Subscribes to the in-process broker for the job with the original request context; jobs.Service.Subscribe checks only that the job belongs to the org.
Every 500 ms re-reads only the job row (deps.Jobs.Get with the org-scoped rctx) to detect status changes; it does not re-check the principal, the token's revocation or the membership.
writeFrame("log", toJobEventDTO(ev)) sends each new job event to a client whose access has since been revoked.

evidence.description: DeactivateUser documents the intended guarantee: it 'ends its access immediately: sessions and API tokens are revoked, not merely flagged for later'; the revocations (lines 522-530) are DB updates only, with no in-process notification to open requests.
RemoveMember deletes the membership row; requireOrg re-reads membership on each new request, but the open stream never calls it again.
The loop ends only on request-context cancellation (client disconnect), a closed subscription, a write error or a terminal job status.

The http.Server sets only ReadHeaderTimeout; there is no WriteTimeout, and internal/api/api.go:371 mounts only RequestID, Logger and Recoverer (no Timeout middleware), so nothing caps the stream's lifetime.
Service.Subscribe checks the org once, at subscription time; the broker then fans out by job id for as long as the subscription lives.
requireOrg's membership read (deps.Tenancy.MembershipOf) is the only membership check on the path, and it runs once per request.

blockers: internal/api tests import internal/api/apitest (testcontainers and the host Docker socket), and requireOrg, membership removal, token revocation and DeactivateUser are all DB-backed, so the stale-stream behaviour cannot be exercised inside the approved network-less sandbox; the claim is source-only.
Whether a fronting reverse proxy in a given deployment enforces its own stream lifetime or idle timeout (which would bound but not remove the window) is outside the repository.

validation_plan.local: In a DB-enabled environment, add an apitest case in internal/api: org owner A and viewer B; create a run job and move it to running (claim it) so it is not terminal; B opens GET /api/v1/orgs/{org}/jobs/{id}/stream with a session cookie (variant: a pxt_ token); read the initial 'status' frame; then A calls DELETE on B's membership (variant: revoke B's token; variant: instance admin POST /api/v1/admin/users/{B}/deactivate); append one job event through the queue's AppendEvent; assert whether B's open stream still receives the 'log' frame within a few poll intervals, and that a fresh GET by B now returns 403/401. The fix re-runs requireOrg (or a cheaper session/token/membership liveness check) on the ticker, e.g. every few ticks, and ends the stream with an error frame on failure; the regression test asserts the stream closes within one check interval after revocation.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed, non-destructive: on a staging instance, start a long-running test play, open its run view as a test viewer, remove that viewer from the org (or deactivate the test user) from another browser, and watch whether log lines keep arriving in the viewer's already-open tab until the run finishes; also note any reverse-proxy stream timeout that closes it earlier.

title: A worker-supplied event timestamp lets one zone's worker keep an org-wide jump host's key-observation state indefinitely
description: When a connection_test job finishes, the manager turns its final run event into a host_connection_tests row. The row's `at` is the RunEvent timestamp the worker sent. grpcsrv eventAt stores it as-is, with no clamp or skew bound against manager time. The row's hop_keys list is checked for shape only: the bastion ids are not checked against the route that the job's claim payload rendered. Bastions belong to the organization, not to a zone, so one jump host can serve routes in several zones. Two consumers pick the newest observation per bastion by `at` across all of the org's tests: the claim-time key-change guard (ListBastionKeyChanged, used by excludeChangedBastions for runs and refuseChangedBastions for bootstrap, rotate_key and revoke_key) and the admin's 'pin what you saw' input and fingerprint display (ListLatestBastionObservations). Connection tests are not refused through a changed bastion, but a genuine test cannot win the newest-by-`at` comparison either. Take a zone worker identity (a compromised worker host, or a play acting as the worker where play-uid separation is off) that is handed a connection_test for one of its own hosts whose route crosses a shared bastion B. The daily re-test hands out such jobs with no user action. Its final event can be dated years ahead with hop_keys=[{bastion_id:B, state:'changed'}]. B then reads as changed for every zone of the org. Runs exclude hosts behind B, and bootstrap, rotate_key and revoke_key claims through B are refused. No later genuine connection test from any zone can supersede the row. Re-pinning does not unblock the bastion by design. No retention, prune or direct DELETE exists for host_connection_tests. The only ways out are to delete the host whose test row carried the injected hop (ON DELETE CASCADE) or to repoint every route and recreate the bastion under a new id. The same future-dated row also stops the daily re-test of the attacker's own host (ListHostsDueForTest) and can plant an attacker fingerprint as the observation an admin is asked to pin. The spec names a zone with its own worker as a trust domain and says a worker is accepted results only for jobs it claimed. This path lets one zone's worker control trust state for a jump host that other zones depend on. The scope stays within one organization: every query filters on the job row's org_id. Naming a bastion that is on none of the worker's own routes would also need that bastion's random UUID, which the worker is not given.
claimed_root_cause: The manager treats a worker-controlled field as a control-plane fact. grpcsrv eventAt keeps RunEvent.at verbatim, appendEvent stores it as job_events.at, and recordTest passes it to hosts.Service.RecordConnectionTest as the observation time of host_connection_tests.at. The newest-by-at selection in ListBastionKeyChanged and ListLatestBastionObservations then lets a single future-dated row stay authoritative for an org-wide bastion indefinitely. A secondary gap widens what can be named: validHops checks only the shape of hop entries, not that each bastion id is on the route the claim rendered for the job.

trace.description: Each RunEvent on the worker's bound RunEvents stream is appended with At: eventAt(ev, s.deps.Clock). The worker is authenticated by mTLS and bound to the job by a one-time token. The timestamp comes from the worker.
A worker-supplied timestamp is returned as ts.AsTime() with no clamp. The manager clock is used only when the field is absent.
ev.At is inserted as job_events.at without bounds.
On the finish path, the newest ok/failed event by seq is read back, with its stored at and payload. The job row supplies only org_id and host_ids.
The worker's at and the payload's hop_keys (any parseable bastion uuid) are passed to the test sink RecordConnectionTest.
validHops filters only on shape (non-nil id, fingerprint present, state unpinned/pinned/changed). The row is created with At: at and the full hop list under the job's org.

The latest observation per bastion is max(at) over the org's test rows that list it as a hop. A 'changed' state on that row marks the bastion changed. hosts.Service.ChangedBastions feeds this to the claim guards refuseChangedBastions and excludeChangedBastions.

evidence.description: eventAt prefers ev.GetAt() over the server clock, with no clamp or skew bound.
validHops validates entry shape only. It does not check that the bastion belongs to the route rendered for the job.
ListLatestBastionObservations orders by t.at, t.id and the service keeps the last row, so a future-dated row is the observation shown for pinning.
A hop state of 'changed' on the latest-by-at row marks the bastion changed.
refuseChangedBastions fails bootstrap, rotate_key and revoke_key claims routed through a changed bastion.
excludeChangedBastions drops every host behind a changed bastion from run claims.
The connection_test kind payload ships the route's bastion ids (and hop credentials) to the claiming worker. A worker learns the ids only of bastions on its own claimed routes.
The bastions table is org-scoped with no zone column, so one bastion can serve routes of every zone.

host_connection_tests rows are removed only by ON DELETE CASCADE from their host. No query deletes or prunes them, so the only remedy is deleting the host that carried the injected test or replacing the bastion.
ListHostsDueForTest skips a host with any test newer than the cut-off, so a future-dated row also ends the daily re-test of the injecting host.

blockers: The decisive behaviour is DB-backed. It needs the newest-by-at selection in ListBastionKeyChanged and ListLatestBastionObservations, the refusal and exclusion of claims through the bastion, and the finding that a later genuine test does not supersede the future-dated row, all on Postgres/TimescaleDB. internal/jobs and internal/hosts store tests need internal/db/testdb (testcontainers on the host Docker socket), which the approved sandbox forbids, so the decisive behaviour was not observed. Source settles the Go path. The eventAt pass-through is source-evident and was not executed.

validation_plan.local: Use a Postgres-enabled test environment (internal/db/testdb) outside this sandbox. Create a dummy org with zones Z1 and Z2, one bastion B (pinned with fingerprint SHA256:genuine) as the zone default of both, and managed hosts H1 in Z1 and H2 in Z2. (1) Enqueue a connection_test for H1, claim it as the Z1 worker through SQLQueue, and append a final 'ok' event with At = now+10y and payload {reachable,auth,sudo,python:true, hop_keys:[{bastion_id:B, fingerprint:'SHA256:x', state:'changed'}]}. Finish it as succeeded. (2) Run a connection_test for H2, claimed by the Z2 worker, and append an event with At = now and hop_keys [{bastion_id:B, fingerprint:'SHA256:genuine', state:'pinned'}]. Finish it. (3) Assert that hosts.Service.ChangedBastions(org,[B]) still returns B and that ListLatestBastionObservations' newest row for B carries 'SHA256:x'. Assert that EnqueueRun plus claim for H2 by the Z2 worker excludes H2, and that a rotate_key claim for H2 fails with ErrHostKeyChanged. Control: repeat step 1 with At = now-1m. Step 2 should then clear B. Delete H1 and confirm B unblocks, which shows the only remedy.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed, non-destructive check on a staging instance with two zones that share one jump host and with dummy hosts only. After the injected test, confirm three things: the jump hosts page keeps showing the injected fingerprint, run and rotate jobs for the other zone's hosts behind that jump host are refused even after a fresh connection test from that zone, and the block lifts only when the injecting zone's host is deleted or the jump host is replaced.

title: An org owner on an instance without mail can pre-create the account for someone else's email and capture that person's later invitations from other organizations
description: When the instance has no outbound mail settings, POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/invites returns the single-use accept_url to the inviting administrator instead of mailing it. POST /api/v1/invites/accept treats the token as proof that the redeemer controls the invited address. On first redemption it creates a user bound to that email with the redeemer's chosen password and opens a session in which the redeemer enrols their own second factor. Any MFA-complete user can create an organization (POST /api/v1/orgs), become its owner, and invite any address. That user can redeem their own link and end up owning a working account for a victim's email that the victim never touched. AcceptInvite later binds every invitation for that address to the existing account on the token alone. If an unrelated organization then invites the real person and she accepts, the membership (up to admin) goes to the attacker-controlled user ID. She gets signed_in=false and cannot sign in, because the password and factor belong to the attacker, who can sign in and holds the invited role in the foreign tenant. The same root cause has a weaker side effect: an inviter holding an accept_url can attach an already-existing account to the inviter's org without its owner's consent.
root_cause: AcceptInvite (internal/tenancy/service.go:398-440) assumes that the invite token proves control of inv.Email; its own doc comment says so at line 378. Service.Invite breaks that assumption. When the mailer returns mail.ErrNotConfigured (lines 363-364), it returns the plaintext link to the inviter, and member_handlers.go:153 sends it back in the API response. The account created when that link is redeemed is then treated as the verified owner of the address for every later invitation: GetUserByEmail (line 418) finds it and AddMembership (line 437) adds the new tenant's membership to it, with no proof from the account holder and no marker that the address was never verified.
intended_behavior: An account should be bound to an email address only by someone who proved control of that mailbox, or it should be marked unverified. Adding a membership to an existing account should require that account's holder to be authenticated, for example with an MFA-complete session whose user ID equals the invited account. An invite token that may have passed through a third party's hands should never be enough.

trace.description: Any MFA-complete session user (requireMFAComplete, line 72) creates an organization. CreateOrg (tenancy/service.go:244) makes the caller its owner, which grants members.manage.
After passing requireOrg(PermMembersManage), the attacker invites victim@corp.example to their own org.

mail.SMTP.Send (wired at app.go:233) returns an error wrapping mail.ErrNotConfigured when setup.LoadSMTP finds no settings (setup/service.go:328). The invitation is kept and inv.AcceptURL is set to the link.
accept_url, which carries the single-use token, is returned to the inviter.

The attacker redeems the token with a password of their choice. AcceptInvite creates the user (service.go:421-427, newAccount=true), and line 241 opens a non-MFA session in which the attacker enrols their own TOTP or passkey through requireEnrolmentSession (mfa_handlers.go:92).

The real person redeems org B's invite. GetUserByEmail returns the attacker-created row, which has a password, so the default branch (lines 429-435) leaves its password and display name unchanged (newAccount=false).
AddMembership(inv.OrgID, u.ID, inv.Role) gives org B's invited role (up to admin) to the attacker-controlled user. The attacker then signs in with their own password and second factor.

evidence.description: The doc comment states the security assumption: 'The invite token only proves control of that mailbox'. The ErrNotConfigured branch breaks it, because the token goes to the inviter.
case errors.Is(sendErr, mail.ErrNotConfigured): inv.AcceptURL = link. The token goes to the inviter, not to the mailbox.

The production mailer's Send (built at app.go:233 from setup.LoadSMTP) wraps ErrNotConfigured whenever no SMTP settings are stored. The setup wizard explicitly treats SMTP as optional (setup/service.go:75-77).
An existing account that has a password is reused silently. AddMembership at line 437 runs without any proof from the account holder.
Org creation is gated only by requireMFAComplete, so any interactive user of the instance can obtain members.manage in an org they own.
AddMembership inserts with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. The membership goes to whichever user row owns the citext-unique email.

conditions.description: The attacker is any MFA-complete session user of the instance (able to create an org through POST /api/v1/orgs), or an admin or owner of any org.

The instance has no stored SMTP settings when the attacker creates the invite. This is the supported 'invite without mail' mode and the state after a setup that skipped mail. Mail may be configured later; the pre-created account persists.
The victim's email address has no account on the instance yet.
Another organization later invites that email address and the real person accepts the invitation.

execution.attacker_perspective: An MFA-complete user who owns an org on an instance without SMTP and targets a person likely to be invited later by a different tenant.
payloads: Independent harness internal/v13harness/v13_test.go (in a scratch copy of the source at b13f3c6): the real tenancy.NewService with an in-memory Store that follows the SQL contract (citext-unique email, atomic single-use TakeInvite, AddMembership ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING), and a Mailer whose Send returns fmt.Errorf("load smtp settings: %w", fmt.Errorf("not found: %w", mail.ErrNotConfigured)), the same shape as SMTP.Send plus setup.LoadSMTP

remediation.strategy: Never treat an account created from a link that was not mailed as an email-verified identity, and never attach a membership to an existing account on the token alone. In AcceptInvite, when the address already belongs to an account with a password, require the request to carry an MFA-complete interactive session whose user ID equals that account; otherwise refuse, without consuming the invite. Optionally, record email verification on users (set only when the link was actually mailed and redeemed) and refuse to reuse an unverified account for another org's invite. Add a regression test: an un-mailed invite redeemed by the inviter, followed by a second org's invite redeemed anonymously, must not add a membership to the first account.

likelihood.reason: Every condition must hold: the instance runs without SMTP when the attacker invites, the target email has no account yet, the attacker is already a user of the shared instance, and another tenant later invites that person, who then accepts.

impact.reason: The attacker gains the invited role, up to admin, in a foreign organization: cross-tenant access to its hosts, runs, members and credential management. The real invitee is shut out of the account that carries their address.

confidence.reason: The full chain is source-traced through the handlers, the service and the SQL contract, and was reproduced independently against the real tenancy.Service with a store fake that follows the documented SQL semantics. Only the HTTP layer and real Postgres were not executed, because those packages are DB-backed and cannot run in the sandbox. Their source (citext UNIQUE email, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, newAccount-gated session) matches the fake.
